book: 051 - Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game

chapters.relation: Andrew Lambert defends the rationality of being a football fan by updating Aristotle: living well in a liberal consumer democracy demands an accessible source of beauty, catharsis, belonging, public discourse, and altruism, and fandom trains exactly these sensibilities — from his childhood prayers for Everton to the 1914 Christmas Truce match and supporters' trusts that own clubs like Exeter City. The mature 'fan of football' takes an ironic view of the 'loyal fan's' tribal passions, gaining the practical wisdom that keeps rivalry (the Liverpool–Everton derby, the 1969 'Football War') from curdling into violence. Fandom thus answers critics who dismiss it as consumerist escapism or bad faith.

chapters.file: ch30 - Don’t Worry, We’ll Be Back Next Season.md
chapters.relation: Vanhoutte argues the derby is not just a game but a clash of identity, territory and honor: old social and religious oppositions (Protestant Rangers v Catholic Celtic, Asian Fenerbahçe v European Galatasaray, Roma v Lazio's championship coffin parade) make derby loyalty a year-round collective identity in which fans win and lose as a 'we', the twelfth player. He traces this to group-identity formation through boundaries dividing the city into 'us' and 'them', showing how belonging produces both derby joy — hugging strangers, 'You'll Never Walk Alone' — and its dark side, from Figo's burnt Barcelona shirt to the Rangers fan murder of a Catholic man. Divisions only turn lethal when exaggerated, so fans must keep the rivalry a game.

Osborne and Coombs turn the Ship of Theseus — every plank replaced, plus Hobbes's reassembled-planks variant — into the 'Aston Villa Paradox': with owner, manager, players, crest and even the shade of claret and blue changed, what makes it the same club fans sing 'Villa till I Die' for? Finding that presentism and Sider's four-dimensionalism cannot say which side on the 2006 pitch was really AVFC, they adopt Lynne Rudder Baker's constitution view: fans create the football-favorable circumstances that constitute a club, so it persists through total replacement of parts as long as supporters keep conferring identity and value — which is why Gareth Barry's value collapsed when he left, and why fans judged Glazer's Manchester United to have stopped existing while welcoming Lerner's Villa.

chapters.file: ch32 - SECOND EXTRA-TIME - Soccer and Society.md
ch33 - I Play Therefore I Am.md
chapters.relation: Foster argues football is inescapably mythic: styles of play embody national self-images, from Victorian England's muscular distrust of artistry to Argentina's criolla viveza and the compadrito, to Sebes's 'socialist' Aranycsapat, while clubs become vessels of nationalism like Athletic Bilbao's Basque-only cantera policy and Barça's 'més que un club'. Myth flows both ways — West Germany's 1954 'Miracle of Berne' restarted German patriotism, and FC Start's 1942 'Death Match' grew into a Soviet martyr myth despite its embellishments — so that, as the chapter concludes with Galeano and McNeill, what people believe matters more to a constructed social reality than what is actually true. Tell me how you play and I'll tell you who you are.

Nguyen asks what makes a team great and answers 'passion', analyzed through the philosophy of mind: passion is a dispositional state — like Stoichkov's love of the game, ascribable even while he sleeps — that manifests occurrently and causally raises the probability of success on a probabilistic theory of causation, though it is neither necessary nor sufficient for winning. The case study is Barcelona's 2008–09 treble: after the meltdown and 'madriditis' before the Bernabéu, Guardiola's passion and code of conduct restored unity, producing the 6–2 clásico, Iniesta's stoppage-time equalizer at Chelsea, and the 2–0 Champions League final win over Manchester United. Passion is what separates the great from the good.

chapters.file: ch35 - A Little bit of Messi for our Life.md
chapters.relation: The authors cast the contrast between disciplined European and improvisational South American football as Mill's struggle between liberty and authority: the coach's tactical orders are 'rules of opinion' the genius may defy, as Maradona did on his sixty-meter run to the Goal of the Century, while the harm principle marks the line at the 'rules of law' — FIFA's Laws of the Game. The Hand of God goal, which broke even a rule of law yet stood because 'a goal is scored when the referee says so', illustrates Searle's point that football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements, leaving a gap filled only by ethics and fair play. Following Wittgenstein's 'ethics and aesthetics are one and the same', they conclude that a bit of Messi-style rule-breaking — Messi replicated both Maradona goals in 2007 — is what makes football, and life, joyful and beautiful.

Imre reads Hungary's Aranycsapat as a political-philosophical event: Sebes's socialist 4–2–4 football was meant to prove that cooperative civil society could flourish under Stalinism, and the 6–3 demolition of England at Wembley, with its self-organizing positional play, became the sporting antithesis to Rákosi's regime — culminating in the 1956 Revolution that Arendt cited as a 'true' revolution of spontaneous councils. The 1954 final loss to West Germany (contrasted with Germany's own rebirth at Berne) entrenched a fatalism that history's organic 'grand narrative' and 'final synthesis' were against Hungary, helping destroy the civil-society possibility the team embodied and pushing Hungarians into anti-politics. His lesson: talent and beauty can be quashed by the contingency of history — igazság, truth-justice, never manifested, and soccer could not overcome history.

Borghini and Baldini analyze how a soccer club becomes a metaphorical mirror constructing its patron's public persona: the sport's unpredictability, its win/lose dialectic, and the referee's undisputed authority make it adaptable as a metaphor for life, and value-laden properties flow from club to owner through a three-step mirroring process from bare individual to owner to persona. They contrast the slowly built stile Juve of the Agnelli family with Silvio Berlusconi, who exploits mass media to link himself only to AC Milan's wins — blaming coaches or his own absence for defeats, like Machiavelli's prince overcoming fortuna — and with Maurizio Zamparini, Palermo's self-styled moral 'Leonidas' demanding democratic rules and safer stadiums. Persona construction emerges as deliberate meaning transfer, not mere image-making.

chapters.file: ch38 - KICKS FROM THE MARK - It’s Down to Penalties.md

chapters.relation: Northcott dissects England's penalty shoot-out misery to ask whether 'bad luck' is objective or a scapegoat: what counts as luck depends on the reasonable standard of preparation, so what was bad luck twenty years ago (no practice) is negligence today, and under Laplace's demon's determinism no sixty-percent chances would exist at all. He rehabilitates objective luck relative to shared standards of reasonableness, concluding that shoot-outs genuinely are more of a lottery than open play — though not a total one. On blame, he uses the deviation-from-default account of causation and Mill's problem of causal selection to argue that singling out a referee over missed open goals or injuries has no objective justification; moral feelings and prejudice pick our scapegoats.

Krnac explains Holland's five missed penalties against Italy at Euro 2000 — Frank de Boer twice, Kluivert, Stam, Bosvelt — through Kierkegaard's The Concept of Anxiety rather than Cruyff's 'chance' or Vergouw's 'poor preparation'. The self, a synthesis of body, mind and spirit (and of the temporal and eternal), must stake itself on a future-oriented choice, but freedom as 'the possibility to be able' makes every free choice an embrace of the unknown, breeding the anxiety that is 'the dizziness of freedom' — visible in de Boer's slide from a five-out-of-ten miss to a lifeless zero that telegraphed his shot to Toldo. Panenka's 1976 chip shows free action chosen without guarantee, while choosing not to choose is itself an evasion of freedom, in penalties as in life.

Saunders rebuts the complaint that penalty shoot-outs are 'lotteries': unlike the coin toss that decided Liverpool–Cologne in 1965, penalties test skill and nerve, and lotteries are not inherently unfair anyway, since giving two equally deserving kidney patients an equal chance is the fairest resort once relevant grounds run out. Fairness does not demand equal chances of winning — it demands due weight to relevant differences — so the better team should be likelier to win, yet winners are not always the better team, as Liverpool's 2005 Istanbul triumph alongside a fifth-place league finish shows. The point of a match is to decide who wins, not who is better, so penalties are legitimate precisely as a skill-testing, exciting way to separate equally deserving teams.

Crowe uses Sartre to explain why refereeing is existentially anguished: in the moment of decision — Grosso's fall over Neill's outstretched legs at the 2006 World Cup — the referee is radically free and solely responsible, and that anguish drives the six familiar referee types into bad faith. The stickler hides behind the letter of Law 12 as Sartre's student hid behind ethical formulas, the ditherer repeats the woman who leaves her hand inert on her date's, the poseur and frustrated player over-act the café waiter's role, and the postman and tough guy play the 'champion of sincerity' who treats character as fixed. The ideal is the authentic referee 'refereeing in the world' — Collina disallowing his own awarded goal at San Siro and explaining why to Inter — who owns his contingency: 'This is what I have chosen.'

chapters.file: ch43 - Football and Religion Don’t Mix.md
chapters.relation: Majeed, writing from Ghana's 2008 Africa Cup of Nations and the Fowl Man affair, argues that 'God is not a referee': a God whose nature is rational, just and good cannot coherently be petitioned to fix match outcomes, so fans who blamed the Fowl Man's bird-charm for the semi-final loss to Cameroon — like players who point skyward à la Kaká — misunderstand both divinity and football. He offers instead an empirical account of winning (strategy, fitness, discipline, fair officiating) topped by irreducible chance, whose illogic even breaks the hypothetical syllogism, since on a lucky day Sheffield United can beat Manchester United. Chance is what keeps football a game at all, and its deeper beauty lies in expressing a common humanity — 'humanity has no boundary' — not in divine intervention.

chapters.file: ch44 - A Phenomenology of Reading the Ref.md
chapters.relation: Vannatta asks what the rules of soccer are from a player's perspective and tests legal theories: natural law and Rawls's veil of ignorance are too abstract to help on the pitch, and Austin's and Hart's positivism overemphasizes FIFA's top-down commands, so the best account is legal pragmatism — Holmes's bad man treats the law as a prophecy of what the ref will actually call, and Dewey roots the rules in custom and in the whistle itself rather than in prior legislation. Husserl's genetic phenomenology then explains how 'reading the ref' is possible: retention and protention synthesized in passive synthesis let experienced players anticipate play — and the referee's tendencies — without deliberation, replacing the impoverished notion of muscle memory. Playing to the whistle becomes a trainable skill of predicting an indeterminate despot, with lessons for coaching and sportsmanship alike.

Grimwood and Miller ask what makes a footballing cliché ('the boy done good', 'a game of two halves', 'they gave 110 percent') hearably meaningful rather than lazy, using Gadamer's hermeneutics and the later Wittgenstein. Gadamer explains clichés as part of the 'horizon' of prejudices that makes understanding the game possible at all — Ian Holloway's taxi-and-young-lady metaphor baffled because it fell outside that horizon — but Wittgenstein goes further: meaning is what words and gestures do in the language-game, so badge-kissing, like the rain dances Wittgenstein defended against Frazer's reductionism, is an expressive form of life whose sincerity or cynicism settles only in context. Even calling something a cliché is itself a move in the game.

holes.name: Collective Identity (us vs them)
holes.what: the formation of group identity through symbolic boundaries separating an 'us' from a 'them', giving members belonging and shared emotion.
holes.why: Chapter 30's whole analysis of derbies — Roma's coffin parade, the Old Firm, Fenerbahçe–Galatasaray — rests on derby fandom as collective identity built on belonging to one side and lasting aversion to the other.

holes.name: Lynne Rudder Baker
holes.what: metaphysician whose 'constitution view' holds that an object (a statue, a dollar bill, a club) is constituted by, but not identical to, its material parts and can persist through their replacement.
holes.why: Chapter 31 uses Baker's unity-without-identity theory as its solution to how Aston Villa remains the same club while owners, managers, players, and crest all change.

holes.name: Mythistory (myth as social reality)
holes.what: the view, associated with William McNeill, that shared myths — whether or not factually true — are symbolic tools that constitute social reality and collective identity.
holes.why: Chapter 33's core claim is that football runs on myth — the Miracle of Berne, Athletic Bilbao's cantera, Barça's més que un club, the FC Start 'Death Match' — and cannot be understood through facts alone.

holes.name: Dispositions and Mental Causation
holes.what: the analysis of mental states such as passion and belief as dispositions rather than occurrent events, and of the mind's causal efficacy in raising the probability of behavior.
holes.why: Chapter 34 explains Barcelona's 2008–09 treble by arguing Guardiola's passion is a disposition whose causal power, understood probabilistically, transformed an underachieving squad.

holes.name: Constitutive and Regulative Rules
holes.what: Searle's distinction (Speech Acts) between rules that create the very activity they govern, like the Laws of the Game, and rules that merely regulate a pre-existing activity.
holes.why: Chapter 35 uses the distinction to show football's regulative capacity cannot guarantee its agreements — hence Maradona's Hand of God stood — leaving a space filled only by ethics and fair play.

holes.name: Nations and Nationalism
holes.what: theories of what constitutes a nation and a national character — shared culture, language, history, or (for Gellner) the organizational needs of industrial modernity.
holes.why: Chapter 36 asks who the Aranycsapat really played for and argues the 1954 World Cup loss and the 1956 Revolution forged and then shattered Hungarian national consciousness.

holes.name: Theory of Metaphor
holes.what: the view that metaphors transfer meaning between 'spheres of discourse' via identity claims, letting one domain shape how another is understood.
holes.why: Chapter 37 explains how soccer clubs act as mirrors: Berlusconi builds a winning public persona by transferring AC Milan's victories to himself and severing its defeats, per the club-as-metaphor logic.

holes.name: Fairness and Equal Claims
holes.what: the normative principle that a contest or distribution is fair when it gives due weight to all relevant claims — treating equals equally without requiring equal chances of winning.
holes.why: Chapter 41's defense of penalty shoot-outs turns on fairness: teams equally deserving after a draw may fairly be separated by an equal-chance procedure such as a lottery or shoot-out.

holes.name: Petitionary Prayer and Divine Attributes
holes.what: the philosophical question whether an omniscient, perfectly just and good God could coherently answer petitions to secure particular worldly outcomes.
holes.why: Chapter 43 argues prayers for football victories are ineffectual because God's just nature cannot prefer teams, making the Fowl Man blame after Ghana's loss misplaced.

holes.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
holes.what: philosopher of philosophical hermeneutics: understanding always proceeds from a historically situated 'horizon' of prejudices that fuses with the horizon of what is interpreted.
holes.why: Chapter 45 uses Gadamer's fusion of horizons to explain how football clichés enable, rather than block, understanding of the game.
